title: Michelson Interferometer
short_intro: The Michelson interferometer is an optical instrument that divides a beam of light into two paths, reflects them back, and recombines them to produce interference fringes. It is used for precise measurements of wavelengths, small refractive index changes, and standard lengths.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic working principle, types of fringes (circular/equal inclination and localized fringes), and wavelength determination using monochromatic sources.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed path difference calculations, visibility of fringes, phase change on reflection, white light fringes, and determination of wavelength difference for closely spaced spectral lines.

prerequisites: Wave theory of light and superposition principle
Path difference and phase difference relationship

concept_notes.heading: Principle of Operation
bullets: A monochromatic light beam is incident on a beam splitter (a partially silvered glass plate) which divides the amplitude into two mutually perpendicular paths.
The two split beams travel towards two plane mirrors, get reflected back, and reunite at the beam splitter to enter the detector or observer's eye.
Interference occurs due to division of amplitude, producing fringes whose shape depends on the alignment and separation of the mirrors.

concept_notes.heading: Types of Fringes
bullets: Circular fringes (Haidinger fringes) are formed when the two reflecting mirrors are strictly parallel, corresponding to interference by equal inclination.
Localized fringes are formed when the mirrors are inclined at an angle, creating an air wedge between one mirror and the virtual image of the other.
White light interference produces only a few colored fringes and a central achromatic dark/bright fringe, useful for finding the zero path difference position.

concept_notes.heading: Role of Compensator Plate
bullets: In white light interferometry, the beam reflected from the beam splitter passes through the glass plate thrice, whereas the transmitted beam passes through it only once.
A compensator plate of identical thickness and material is placed in the path of the transmitted beam to equalize the optical path in glass for both arms.
Without the compensator plate, white light fringes cannot be observed due to dispersion and unequal optical paths.

concept_notes.heading: Applications
bullets: Measurement of the wavelength of monochromatic light with high precision.
Determination of the refractive index of thin transparent films or gases.
Historical significance in proving the non-existence of the luminiferous ether via the Michelson-Morley experiment.

derivations.title: Path Difference for Circular Fringes
derivations.conditions: Mirrors M1 and M2 are exactly perpendicular, and the effective air film thickness between M1 and the virtual image M2' is d.
steps: Consider a ray of light entering at an angle of incidence i to the air film of thickness d.
The path difference between the two interfering beams is given by Delta = 2d cos(theta), where theta is the angle of refraction inside the film.

Accounting for a phase change of pi (or lambda/2) due to reflection from the denser medium (the silvered surface of the beam splitter), the effective path difference becomes Delta = 2d cos(theta) +/- lambda/2.
derivations.result: 2d cos(theta) = m\lambda for bright fringes and 2d cos(theta) = (m + 1/2)\lambda for dark fringes

derivations.title: Wavelength Determination Derivation
derivations.conditions: Mirror M1 is translated by a distance delta d to shift N circular fringes past the crosshair.
steps: For the center of the interference pattern (theta = 0, cos(theta) = 1), the condition for a bright fringe of order m is 2d = m\lambda.
When mirror M1 is moved by delta d, the thickness changes to d + delta d, and a new fringe order m - N is observed at the center: 2(d + delta d) = (m - N)\lambda.
Subtracting the two equations yields 2 delta d = N\lambda, which allows calculation of lambda.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Circular Fringes Pattern
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Concentric bright and dark rings whose spacing decreases outward from the center.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents loci of constant angle of incidence (Haidinger fringes); rings crowd together at larger angles because cos(theta) varies non-linearly.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual questions on fringe spacing variation and mirror alignment.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Localized Straight Fringes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parallel, equidistant straight fringes formed when mirrors are inclined.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents an air wedge interference pattern localized in the plane of the mirrors.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to explain measurement of wedge angle and surface flatness testing.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fringe Visibility Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A periodically modulating amplitude curve showing peaks and nodes as mirror displacement increases for a doublet source.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the superposition of two sets of interference patterns going in and out of phase, used to measure hyperfine splitting or doublet separation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT numerical and conceptual graph analysis.

solved_numericals.question: In a Michelson interferometer, when the movable mirror is displaced by 0.294 mm, 1000 fringes cross the field of view. Calculate the wavelength of light used.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Delta d = 0.294 mm = 0.294 \times 10^-3 m, N = 1000.
Use the formula lambda = (2 * Delta d) / N.

solved_numericals.question: A transparent tube of length 10 cm filled with air is placed in one arm of a Michelson interferometer using light of wavelength 589 nm. When the air is evacuated, 70 fringes shift past the crosshair. Calculate the refractive index of air.
solution_steps: Identify given values: t = 10 cm = 0.1 m, lambda = 589 \times 10^-9 m, N = 70.
Rearrange for refractive index: mu = 1 + (N * lambda) / (2 * t).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the wavelength difference delta lambda for the sodium yellow doublet (mean wavelength 589 nm) if the visibility of the fringes drops to a minimum when the mirror is moved by 0.294 mm.
solution_steps: Identify given values: lambda = 589 \times 10^-9 m, d = 0.294 mm = 2.94 \times 10^-4 m.
Use the formula for doublet separation: delta lambda = lambda^2 / (2 * d).
Calculate result: delta lambda = (3.469 \times 10^-13) / (5.88 \times 10^-4) = 5.90 \times 10^-10 m = 0.59 nm.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Light sources are assumed to possess sufficient temporal coherence to produce stable interference over the path difference introduced.
Limitation: Extended sources are required to observe circular fringes, and path difference cannot exceed the coherence length of the source.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Michelson interferometer relies on division of wavefront.
common_misconceptions.correct: It relies on division of amplitude.
common_misconceptions.why: A beam splitter divides the amplitude of a single incoming wavefront into two parts, which travel along different arms and then interfere.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Circular fringes are localized at the surface of the mirror.
common_misconceptions.correct: Circular fringes are localized at infinity (or viewed through a telescope focused to infinity).
common_misconceptions.why: They are fringes of equal inclination (Haidinger fringes) formed by rays emerging at the same angle.

quick_revision: Michelson interferometer works on division of amplitude to produce circular or localized interference fringes.
